blocks.en: Following stress detection and optogenetic signal delivery, the next stage of ReLEAF is biological production. Our system uses engineered B. subtilis WB800 as the microbial chassis for producing plant-protective molecules in response to a controlled light signal. However, as the light inducible system is still being tested, we needed a separate circuit to obtain the protectants rapidly for subsequent functional assays.

blocks.en: Figure 8. Effect of electroporation voltage on transformation of Bacillus subtilis WB800 carrying the pVeg-SamyQ:AcdS 2.1 construct. Bacillus subtilis strain WB800 was transformed with plasmid construct Pveg-SamyQ-AcdS-2.1 and plated on LB or erythromycin-containing LB agar plate under varying electroporation voltages and dilution conditions. Plating at a 1:2 000 000 dilution yielded high colony density under (A) 2.1 kV yielding 434 colonies, (B) 2.3 kV yielding 403 colonies. In contrast, applying a voltage of 2.3 kV pulse on erythromycin-containing LB agar conditions (C) resulted in a sharp decline in viability, yielding 15 colonies due to excessive electrical field strength and cell lysis. Plating undiluted cells on erythromycin-containing LB agar plate following a 2.1 kV pulse (D) yields 16 colonies, demonstrating significantly fewer isolated transformants under otherwise identical pulse parameters. Based on the experimental data, 2.1 kV is the optimal electroporation voltage for transforming Bacillus subtilis WB800 with this construct. blocks.en: To examine and quantify the secretion of our protectants, we performed three assays to evaluate protectant secretion, quantify protein concentration, and assess enzymatic activity. Each protectant contains a His-tag according to our construct design, allowing us to detect the target proteins by western blotting and assess their presence based on their expected molecular weights. Meanwhile, DNPH works alongside western blot to allow us to quantify the enzyme activity, determining how much active protectant is produced under the varying constructs of our engineered bacteria, with the different signal peptides. Specifically, one of our target protectants ACC deaminase is an enzyme that catalyzes the deamination of 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate (ACC), which we can then use the assay to detect the enzyme activity of the protein secreted by our engineered Bacillus subtilis.

blocks.en: The construct we focus on most is for the protectant ACC deaminase, as the protectant highlights the results of our codon optimization. For the comparison, we have two constructs that vary in both the secretory signal peptide (Csn and SamyQ) fused with the ACC deaminase gene sequence (wild type vs codon-optimized v2t1). We quantify the ACC deaminase in culture supernatants by anti-His ELISA to compare the expression and secretion of the variant gene sequences. Though the variance in the signal peptide does influence the measured results, due to time constraints we were unable to account for the variance through new wet lab cloning. To isolate the visualization of the codon optimization, the signal peptide contribution is accounted for using published quantitative data. Though documented values are limited and come from different research: the native Csn signal peptide mediated 33.8% secretion of its cognate cargo within an E. coli system [9], while reaching near 72% of the best signal peptide within a 173-member B. subtilis library for cutinase [10]. Meanwhile, SamyQ has been reported to reach around 90% secretion of a heterologous α-amylase within B. subtilis [11]. Since the two signal peptides have not been directly compared in a single experiment, nor has either been documented with ACC deaminase, we present the codon optimization as a range calculated by dividing the raw concentration by the OD600 and then dividing the value by the signal peptide correction value of 90%/33.8% = 2.66.

blocks.en: The chromoprotein reporter
blocks.text: The chromoprotein reporter

blocks.en: In our project, AmilCP is a chromoprotein which serves as a reporter to visualize and quantify the successful secretion of the target protein from our engineered Bacillus subtilis in both the LPA and bioreactor. Since AmilCP displays a blue/purple hue, we are able to utilize absorbance as a quantifiable and more direct readout compared to biochemical assays. Considering feasibility, the enzymatic assay for ACCD requires DNPH that is hazardous to handle, as well as additional time and resources. Fluorescence-based reporters were not feasible, as we could not obtain a fluorescence microplate reader. Western blotting and ELISA are also time-consuming and costly. Therefore, a chromoprotein was convenient for us to verify the success of secretion.

blocks.en: A likely explanation for the lack of results is because of the folding of AmilCP, as the secretion of proteins of the originating Bacillus family has been well documented within literature to become severely damaged due to the bottlenecks in secretion pathways, often caused by slow or incompatible folding [13]. Taking this into consideration, AmilCP is a β-barrel chromoprotein that folds rapidly in the cytoplasm, which may explain the inefficient secretion, because the Sec pathway in B. subtilis requires proteins to remain unfolded during translocation [12]. We therefore reasoned that AmilCP and other chromoproteins cannot be secreted efficiently due to the incompatibility between the bacteria and proteins, and transferred our focus towards GanA.

blocks.en: We have successfully assembled our optogenetic circuit, which combines a red/green light-sensing system that converts light into a gene expression signal with a module producing our target protectant, either ACCD or ACCD 2.1 (Figures 5 and 6). The cells are therefore built to respond to light. Following our successful cloning of our Level 1 Green-Light Responsive Module, we then inserted this construct into a Level 2 vector alongside our PCB Production Module, Light Sensing Module and Transcriptional Module to form our complete optogenetic system. blocks.en: The Light Plate Apparatus (LPA) is an open-source hardware, a 24-well plate with an independently programmable LED under each well, so identical cultures can be held at different red and green light intensities in one experiment. We used it to check whether light can act as a reliable dial for protectant production; we checked whether 2%, 12% and 100% light gives clearly separated levels of expression, and whether any setting slows growth. blocks.en: Since the L2-Csn-AcdS (ABDI) construct had been successfully assembled, we first used it to test whether light intensity and exposure time would affect the amount of protectant produced. The LPA was used to deliver light-on and light-off signals. Cultures were placed directly into the LPA and sampled every 2 hr from 0 to 8 hr (Figure 19). The data showed an increase in protectant expression with increasing green-light intensity, and expression also increased over time. Taken together, these results suggest that our optogenetic circuit is functional. However, the red light group also showed high expression, comparable to that of the highest green light intensity. This may be due to spectral leakage from the green channel into the red channel. In addition, the ABDI strain could not be recovered from glycerol stock, so every repeat required fresh electroporation. We therefore switched to the codon-optimized AcdS 2.1 (ABDQ), which does not have this problem.

blocks.en: Following the western blot results, ELISA and DNPH assays were introduced as more precise quantitative methods to measure ACCD accumulation and activity under short term and long term light induction. Competitive ELISA replaced the Western blot and estimated how much ACCD was in each sample, as a concentration. The DNPH assay measured ACCD activity by detecting α-ketobutyrate (α-KB), the product of the enzyme, and so showed whether the ACCD works. Running both on the same samples separated how much ACCD was present from how active it was. We ran them in two sets of experiments.

blocks.en: The ELISA showed no change over time. ACCD was already present at the baseline (about 3.0 µg/mL before illumination) and measured 2.6 to 3.2 µg/mL at every time point under both colors, well above the plasmid-free control (about 1.3 µg/mL), indicating that the cultures produced ACCD but the amount did not rise with light (Figure 22). In contrast, the DNPH assay showed an increase in activity. Activity rose from the baseline (about 2.7 on the plotted axis) to about 18 under green light and 16 under red light by 8 h, and green was higher than red at every time point (about 8 vs 6 at 3 h, 12 vs 9 at 6 h and 18 vs 16 at 8 h; Figure 23). However, the gap was clearest at 6 h, and the error bars overlapped at 3 h and 8 h. Taken together, the amount of His-tagged ACCD stayed the same while its activity kept rising and leaned toward green. This may be because the protein takes time to become active: the ELISA counts the His-tagged protein whether or not it is working, whereas the DNPH assay only detects the active enzyme. We have not tested this directly.

blocks.en: What it settles
blocks.text: What it settles

blocks.en: The light plate delivered red and green light to the Bacillus subtilis cultures without slowing growth: at 100% intensity, both colors grew alike through 8 h and reached an OD600 of about 1.0 at 24 h (1.026 red, 1.017 green). On Western blots, the original ABDI construct gave an unclear result because the red 100% reference also showed its strongest band at 8 h, so we switched to the codon optimized ABDQ construct. With ABDQ, green light alone switched ACCD expression on, and green lanes were somewhat stronger than red at 13 h and 16 h, although the difference was small and not yet quantified. ELISA and the DNPH assay then gave more precise readings. In the short-term set, the amount of His-tagged ACCD stayed flat while its activity rose over time and leaned toward green, which may be because the protein takes time to become active. In the long-term set, ACCD amounts were again similar under both colors, and the high green-light activity at 13 h was not maintained at 16 h. The similar ELISA values across conditions may be due to too many samples in the LPA at once, so that light from neighboring wells affected each other. In addition, CcaSR needs red light at about 672 nm to switch off, but our red LEDs emit at 640 nm, which may be why red light did not turn expression off efficiently. We have not tested either explanation directly. Taken together, these results suggest that the plate can serve as our light-control platform and that ABDQ is expressed under green light, but they do not yet show a clean, graded response to light intensity. Before relying on light as a control signal, we will quantify the blots against a loading control, add a WB800 lane without the plasmid, and repeat the ELISA and DNPH assays with biological replicates.

blocks.en: Run 3 served as our endurance test, demonstrating the photometer's ability to monitor a culture continuously for over 18 days without manual sampling. Over 434.2 hours, the system recorded measurements every ten minutes, producing 2671 valid readings out of 2720. However, the reference beam began showing irregular fluctuations around 220 hours, and the optical density measurements became unreliable at 243.0 hours, with variability increasing five- to tenfold. This failure provided valuable data for developing the fault detection model described in Stress detection, which identified the issue at 216.3 hours, before the measurement channel became unusable.

blocks.en: To address these issues, we made two improvements for run 6: reducing the permeate flow rate from 24 to 12 mL/min and introducing an acceptance filter that retained the last valid reading when measurements failed quality checks. Of the 1083 measurement windows, 31 were rejected, none exceeded 20% bubbles, and reference signal variation remained within 17%. These improvements produced a stable OD600 curve, increasing from 0.14 to 2.71 over 37 hours. Beyond approximately 2.7, the sample signal dropped to one-tenth of the reference, triggering a low-signal warning and indicating the instrument's upper measurement limit under these conditions.

blocks.en: To determine whether the photometer responded predictably to increasing turbidity, we calibrated it against two different particulate standards. Each provided a nonliving turbidity reference, allowing us to characterize the optical response independently of changes in microbial growth, and testing a second material allowed us to evaluate whether the relationship observed with the first was reproducible.

blocks.en: The inline photometer showed strong agreement with the BioDrop spectrophotometer in both calibration experiments. blocks.en: The SiO₂ experiment provided further evidence of measurement consistency through a dilution and recovery test at 137.6 minutes. These results demonstrate that the photometer responded proportionally to changes in particle concentration and recovered its original reading when the concentration was restored, supporting its use for comparing measurements over time.

blocks.en: To evaluate the production of our engineered bioprotectants, we used competitive ELISA to estimate the concentrations of His-tagged ACC deaminase (ACCD), LEA14, and BoPep4 in bacterial culture samples. The assay provided a quantitative measure of detectable recombinant protein, complementing Western blot analysis and enzymatic activity assays. By comparing the estimated protein concentrations across different constructs and experimental conditions, we aimed to assess bioprotectant production and identify potential differences in expression and secretion.

blocks.en: Competitive ELISA was used to compare apparent His-tagged protein concentrations across ACCD, LEA14, and BoPep4 expression constructs at 8 and 12 hours. Among the tested constructs, Csn-ACCD showed the highest estimated concentrations, increasing from 12.072 µg/mL at 8 hours to 13.446 µg/mL at 12 hours. Csn-LEA exhibited relatively similar concentrations at both time points (6.323 and 6.090 µg/mL), while the BoPep4 variants displayed different temporal patterns. Notably, BoPep4 v2t1 increased from 5.230 to 6.323 µg/mL, whereas the original BoPep4 construct decreased from 6.090 to 4.744 µg/mL. The WB800 control also produced detectable assay signals, indicating that the estimated concentrations should not be interpreted as recombinant protein-specific yields without additional validation. Furthermore, several calculated concentrations exceeded the standard-curve range, limiting the reliability of absolute quantification. Together, these measurements provide a preliminary comparison of apparent protein abundance across the engineered constructs.

blocks.en: Without exogenous PLP supplementation, the csn strain exhibits product output nearly identical to the WB800 baseline, suggesting that its endogenous ACCD activity is negligible relative to the host background. Adding PLP significantly enhances csn performance, increasing total product output by 13.7 nmol (+0.119 mM alpha-ketobutyrate) above the WB800 baseline, demonstrating the importance of PLP supplementation for optimal ACCD activity. blocks.en: Across the 36 hour run, the extracellular alpha-ketobutyrate accumulation shows a phase-dependent kinetics. Starting from a baseline concentration of −0.0399 mM at 1 hour (OD 540 nm = −0.015), the active enzyme secretion initiated by 6 hours (0.0333 mM, OD 540 nm = 0.003) and maintained steady accumulation through 12 hours (0.0293 mM, OD 540 nm = 0.002). blocks.en: Agar-based salinity stress
blocks.text: Agar-based salinity stress

blocks.en: To evaluate the efficacy of our engineered plant protectants in a controlled environment, we established an agar-based screening pipeline utilizing Arabidopsis thaliana as our standard model organism. The primary goal of these agar assays was to determine whether exogenous application of our protectants, such as ACC deaminase, LEA14, and BoPep4, could mitigate the adverse phenotypic and biochemical effects of salt stress. To maximize data accuracy and reproducibility, while monitoring and ranging protectants' application timing, we deployed the horizontal agar system as our platform. Initial gradient testing identified 100 mM NaCl as the optimal baseline stress concentration, severe enough to induce inhibition of plant growth without causing immediate systemic lethality.

The primary goal of these agar assays was to determine whether exogenous application of our protectants, such as ACC deaminase, LEA14, and BoPep4, could mitigate the adverse phenotypic and biochemical effects of salt stress. To maximize data accuracy and reproducibility, while monitoring and ranging protectants' application timing, we deployed the horizontal agar system as our platform. Initial gradient testing identified 100 mM NaCl as the optimal baseline stress concentration, severe enough to induce inhibition of plant growth without causing immediate systemic lethality.

blocks.en: Following the successful production and secretion of ACC deaminase (ACCD) from our engineered biological systems, we conducted targeted biological assays to evaluate whether the purified enzyme retains measurable enzymatic and protective function on plants under abiotic stress. Initial plate screenings evaluating filter-sterilized ACCD across different treatment timings (0, 75, 100 mM NaCl) revealed moderate rescue effectiveness. Although overall phenotypic improvements were modest due to baseline plate contamination during early filtering trials, post-treatment groups subjected to salt stress exhibited visible recovery comparable to baseline controls.

blocks.en: Under non-stressed conditions, 75 mM and 100 mM NaCl control groups show relevant chlorosis characterized by white and yellow leaves (Figure 42e, j), consistent with the applied salt stress. Despite contamination, all pre-treatment ACC deaminase groups showed the greater rosette area, dense foliage, and more extensive petioles and root growth (Figure 42b, f, j). Under the pre-treatment ACCD 100 mM NaCl group, leaves turned slightly yellow or white, and showed anthocyanin accumulation (Figure 42j), while pre-treatment ACCD with 75 mM NaCl plants also show slight chlorosis, overall still retaining the majority of chlorophyll pigments. Under groups treated with ACC deaminase at co-treatment timing, as salt stress concentration progressively increases from 0 to 100 mM, seedlings showed severe inhibition of plant growth under salinity stress (Figure 42g, k). This result indicates that pre-treatment or post-treatment of ACC deaminase showed rescue effect rather than co-treatment.

blocks.en: Phenotypic observation of the BoPep4 co-treated plates (Figure 44b, e, h) shows progressive salt damage as the NaCl concentration increases from 0 to 100 mM. At 100 mM NaCl, this damage is characterized by extensive chlorosis, with yellow-to-green leaf margins, and partial leaf bleaching. In addition, every BoPep4 co-treated plate shows a green-to-yellow gradient from leaf to leaf, with round, spatulate leaves. blocks.en: Salt behaves differently in soil platforms compared to the agar trials; therefore, the salinity concentrations and protectant doses are required to be evaluated and fine tuned to allow for maximum observation differences in rescue effectiveness. We evaluated two established soil salinization protocols on 2-week-old Arabidopsis thaliana in growth chambers, including a top-down wash method using 100, 200, and 300 mM NaCl solutions and a sub-irrigation accumulation method. While initial trials with gradual ramps or subirrigation resulted in insufficient stress due to freshwater flushing and ion leaching, we resolved these hydrological challenges by implementing a sequential top-drenching protocol. We apply equal volumes from 30 to 50 mL per pot of 100 mM, 200 mM, and 300 mM NaCl consecutively without intermediate freshwater irrigation. Bottom tray reservoirs were maintained at a depth of 1 to 2 cm around 200 to 400 mL to keep the root zone in continuous equilibrium, establishing an optimal soil stress model to evaluate the protective efficacy of engineered microbial protectants across pre-treatment, co-treatment, and post-treatment windows.

blocks.en: Transitioning heat stress assays into soil platforms requires re-evaluating incubation parameters and application regimens, as thermal responses in soil differ significantly from controlled agar trials. We adapted established thermo-priming frameworks to 2-week-old Arabidopsis thaliana grown in soil by exposing plants to 37 °C for 5 days in an incubator, followed by a 5-day recovery period at 22 to 25 °C in a growth chamber, to establish optimal parameters for testing engineered microbial protectants such as ACC deaminase. We systematically evaluate three application timings relative to heat exposure: pre-treatment to initiate cellular priming, co-treatment applied during heat exposure, and post-treatment during recovery, measuring post-stress survival, vegetative growth, chlorophyll retention, and anthocyanin accumulation.

blocks.en: The hollow-fiber membrane (HFM) module divides the system into a cell-containing lumen loop and a cell-free shell compartment, allowing secreted ACC deaminase (ACCD) to be recovered from the shell permeate without discharging the engineered Bacillus subtilis.
blocks.text: The hollow-fiber membrane (HFM) module divides the system into a cell-containing lumen loop and a cell-free shell compartment, allowing secreted ACC deaminase (ACCD) to be recovered from the shell permeate without discharging the engineered Bacillus subtilis.

blocks.en: The lumen loop draws culture from a magnetically stirred medium reservoir and carries it through a peristaltic pump, an inline flow meter, an inline photometer, and the HFM module before returning it to the reservoir through a vent filter. Three pressure transducers report feed (lumen inlet), retentate (lumen outlet), and permeate (shell) pressure (Figure 56). The shell compartment is closed except for a single outlet that discharges into a dedicated collection bottle, so permeate leaves the system only when that valve is opened. In the final configuration, the valve is servo-actuated, so material is harvested on demand rather than as a continuous bleed.

blocks.en: The containment mechanism relies on the difference between bacterial cell size and membrane pore size. Rod-shaped B. subtilis cells typically measure 0.8 to 2.0 µm in width and up to 3.0 µm in length, making them substantially larger than the membrane's 0.2 µm pores. Smaller particles, however, including cellular debris and vesicles measuring 20 to 200 nm, may still pass through the membrane alongside secreted proteins.

The integrated system sustained B. subtilis for 116 h in a single continuous run, with the inline photometer resolving the full growth curve from inoculation to a final OD600 of approximately 3.7 (Figure 59).

blocks.en: The first integrated cycle was run at 37 °C in 500 mL of medium, using B. subtilis 168 carrying pSTK-EXP1-Pveg-Csn:Acds, a vector that constitutively expresses ACCD, with erythromycin at 5 µg/mL. Growth was continuous rather than batch-limited: OD600 rose steadily to a first plateau at approximately 40 h, the point at which ACCD accumulation was greatest. blocks.en: Reliable inline optical density required two mechanical corrections. In the second cycle the OD600 trace was unstable throughout the run, and the cycle was terminated early (Figure 61). We attributed this to the short tubing connecting the inline photometer, which transmitted pump vibration directly to the optical head and displaced the optical axis. In the third cycle, the tubing separating the photometer from both the HFM module and the flow meter was extended to 30 cm, and the medium volume was reduced from 1 L to 500 mL to raise the surface-area-to-biomass ratio for oxygen diffusion. The OD600 and pH records from that cycle were stable and internally consistent up to the point of mechanical failure at 38 h (Figure 62), establishing the inline photometer as a usable continuous growth sensor.

blocks.en: pH and antibiotic resupply
blocks.text: pH and antibiotic resupply

blocks.en: pH regulation and antibiotic resupply are both required for sustained, reproducible culture. Growth slowdown in the HFM bioreactor coincided with the fall of lumen pH to 6.5, and restoring pH together with antibiotic eliminated both the slowdown and the spurious second exponential phase, yielding a classical growth curve over 80 h (Figure 63).

Growth slowdown in the HFM bioreactor coincided with the fall of lumen pH to 6.5, and restoring pH together with antibiotic eliminated both the slowdown and the spurious second exponential phase, yielding a classical growth curve over 80 h (Figure 63).

blocks.en: The direction of the pH drift was initially unclear. In the second cycle, pH rose over the run, against expectation for continuous culture; few bubbles were visible in the reservoir at the time, so insufficient oxygen supply was suspected and the working volume was reduced from 1 L to 500 mL for the next cycle. With all sensors functioning in the third cycle, pH instead fell monotonically from about 6.9 to 6.4 (Figure 62). Superimposing the growth and pH profiles showed that the inflection in the OD600 curve occurred at the point where pH crossed 6.5. Since Bacillus subtilis growth and the structural stability of the protectant enzyme are both impaired below pH 6.5, and pH above 7.5 is also unfavorable, lumen pH needs to be within this window rather than just monitored passively. Because the crossing can occur outside working hours, automated correction was made a design requirement for the following cycle.

blocks.en: Automated pH control was implemented in the fourth cycle as a feedback loop on the feeding valve. A peristaltic pump with a maximum flow rate of approximately 60 mL/min was installed upstream of the feeding Luer valve. When lumen pH fell to 6.8, the controller dosed 5 mL of 1 M KOH per minute until pH returned to 7.0. The loop operated as designed for the first night of the run, after which 1 M KOH was found to be corroding the feeding valve. Automated dosing was therefore withdrawn, and pH was corrected manually once per day by adding 20 mL KOH mixed with 25 mL TB medium and supplemented with 100 µL of 25 mg/mL erythromycin.

blocks.en: The resulting profile is the most complete growth record obtained from the system (Figure 63). Exponential growth occupied 2 to 9 h, after which OD600 rose slowly and monotonically to approximately 3.3 by 80 h. pH traced a sawtooth between roughly 6.4 and 7.9, each sharp rise corresponding to a base addition and each decay to subsequent acidification by the culture. Critically, the second exponential phase seen in earlier cycles did not reappear. Because the daily feed supplied erythromycin alongside base, this supports the interpretation that the earlier second rise reflected loss of the selection marker rather than a genuine metabolic transition, and it establishes antibiotic resupply, not only pH correction, as a requirement for long-term operation.

blocks.en: The corrosion finding constrains the chemistry of the feed line. Two candidates could have attacked the feeding valve: 35% hydrogen peroxide from the CIP procedure and 1 M KOH from pH adjustment. Both circulate through the same fitting, so the cycles reported here cannot tell them apart. Before we can bring automated dosing back, we need either a milder base or a valve body that resists it.

blocks.en: Pressure and sampling
blocks.text: Pressure and sampling

blocks.en: Valve-controlled transmembrane pressure drives permeate across the membrane and enables timed shell-side sampling. Coordinated actuation of the shell valve and the pinch valve raised mean transmembrane pressure (TMP) from approximately 0.03 bar to 0.16 bar for 60 s, yielding 20 to 30 mL of shell permeate per sampling event without interrupting the culture (Figure 64).
blocks.text: Valve-controlled transmembrane pressure drives permeate across the membrane and enables timed shell-side sampling. Coordinated actuation of the shell valve and the pinch valve raised mean transmembrane pressure (TMP) from approximately 0.03 bar to 0.16 bar for 60 s, yielding 20 to 30 mL of shell permeate per sampling event without interrupting the culture (Figure 64).

blocks.en: Under normal operation the feed (lumen inlet), retentate (lumen outlet) and permeate (shell) pressures sat at approximately 0.16, 0.025 and 0.065 bar g respectively, giving a mean TMP near 0.03 bar. The peristaltic pump imposed a periodic pulsation on TMP whose troughs reached negative values (Figure 64B). This briefly pulled fluid from the shell side back into the lumen, then pushed it out again. The back-and-forth flow kept the shell space from sitting as dead volume.

blocks.en: Sampling followed a set sequence. We shortened the sensor logging interval from 300 s to 5 s to catch the full pressure transient. Opening the shell-side valve to the collection bottle vented the shell space to atmosphere and dropped the permeate reading to near 0 bar. The pinch valve then closed off the tubing between the HFM outlet and the reservoir inlet for 60 s. Feed pressure rose to about 0.245 bar and retentate pressure to about 0.10 bar, which brought mean TMP to about 0.16 bar. Lumen flow dropped only slightly during occlusion, from about 305 to 285 mL/min (Figure 64C). We then released the pinch valve and closed the shell valve, and all three pressures returned to their pre-sampling values. The pressure record shows directly that the pinch valve supplies the driving force for filtration, not the pump's residual pressure gradient.

blocks.en: Pressure monitoring alone was insufficient to detect loss of containment. Leakage occurred at the feeding Luer valve, located at the serum bottle inlet, the lowest-pressure point in the loop. Contrary to expectation, lumen pressure rose rather than fell when the valve failed: feed pressure climbed from approximately 0.19 to 0.37 bar, while TMP showed no significant change (Figure 65). Pressure signatures are therefore diagnostic of this fault only in combination with other channels, and a dedicated leak-detection device is required for unattended operation.

blocks.en: Secreted ACC deaminase accumulates in the shell permeate and becomes catalytically active after 18 h. Shell permeate contained secreted ACCD above 2 µg/mL throughout a 72 h run, and the enzyme was catalytically active from 18 h, with specific activity rising to 6 to 8 U/mg and remaining at that level through the end of the run (Figure 67).

ELISA showed ACCD above 2 µg/mL at every time point, peaking at about 6.5 µg/mL at 12 h and settling to 2.5 to 3 µg/mL after 36 h (Figure 67A). The 1 h signal is most likely carry-over from the overnight primary culture used as inoculum rather than protein produced in the reactor.

blocks.en: Our data shows that activity lagged behind protein accumulation. The DNPH assay we conducted measures α-ketobutyrate (α-KB) released from ACC; it gave only marginal activity at 6 and 12 h, rose sharply at 18 h, and remained stable thereafter (Figure 67B). One unit (U) is the amount of enzyme releasing 1 µmol α-KB per hour under the assay conditions used here (30 °C, 12 h incubation), and 1 mU = 0.001 U. Normalizing to ELISA concentration gives specific activity below 1 U/mg at 6 to 12 h, rising to 6.3 U/mg at 18 h and holding between 5 and 8.4 U/mg through 72 h (Figure 67C). Therefore, immunoreactive protein appears before functional enzyme.

blocks.en: We think the lag comes from post-secretory maturation. ACCD only works as a multimer and needs pyridoxal 5′-phosphate as a cofactor. Neither oligomer assembly nor cofactor loading is likely to happen right away once the protein crosses into the extracellular space. Specific activity then plateaus, which suggests maturation keeps up with secretion for the rest of the run.
